title: Exact and Approximate Algorithms for Polytree Learning
claim: A reduction maps set-partitioning elements and a connecting node onto choice nodes whose parent-set choices encode the combinatorial solution.
layout: Single panel, two node groups top and bottom, colored arrows converge on one node
description: A schematic of a hardness reduction. A boxed row at the top holds universe nodes u_1, u_2, u_3, ..., u_n' drawn as black dots. To its right sits a lone connecting node p, labeled as able to take only the empty parent set. Below, a wide box holds choice nodes s_1, s_2, s_3, ..., s_{t'-1}, plus a separate small box with s_t'. These are labeled as able to take non-empty parent sets. Red arrows from u_1 and u_2, blue arrows from u_3 and u_n', and a black arrow from p all converge on s_2, showing its chosen parent set. Curly braces on the right and below give role labels and the parent-set sizes S^{1/ε} and S^{t-(t'-1)1/ε}. The converging colored arrows draw the eye first.

Then the choice node s2 gets a parent set of S1/ϵ = S2 which consists of the connecting node p and the two sets {u1, u2} (in red) and {u3, un′} (in blue) of the k′-SET PARTITIONING instance and this gives score 2.
abstract: Polytrees are a subclass of Bayesian networks that seek to capture the conditional dependencies between a set of $n$ variables as a directed forest and are motivated by their more efficient inference and improved interpretability. Since the problem of learning the best polytree is NP-hard, we study which restrictions make it more tractable by considering for example in-degree bounds, properties of score functions measuring the quality of a polytree, and approximation algorithms. We devise an algorithm that finds the optimal polytree in time $O((2+Îµ)^n)$ for arbitrarily small $Îµ> 0$ and any constant in-degree bound $k$, improving over the fastest previously known algorithm of time complexity $O(3^n)$. We further give polynomial-time algorithms for finding a polytree whose score is within a factor of $k$ from the optimal one for arbitrary scores and a factor of $2$ for additive ones. Many of the results are complemented by (nearly) tight lower bounds for either the time complexity or the approximation factors.
